blocks.text: INT-06 · Rhetoric of public speeches
Lesson overview

Speeches of Heads of State and Government, interventions to the United Nations and the League of Arab States, speeches for national holidays, inaugurations, election campaigns: the Arab rhetorical tradition is ancient and still alive, and a public speech in Arabic uses resources that institutional Italian uses less: parallelism, antithesis, repetition, prose rhyme, citation, titles of protocol. Knowing them serves to understand what the speech wants to achieve, to distinguish between what is promised and what is only evoked, and to translate without flattening or inflating the text. In this unit learn the main rhetorical figures and their Arabic names, protocol formulas, a method of analysis in five questions, and work on invented speeches and on a real public discourse chosen from institutional sources (Appendix C). The work is of linguistic analysis: no political judgement is required. Two weeks.

rows: B2-09 (modality), B2-10 (explanation), B2-11 (connotation), B2-14 (formulas and titles), B2-22 (exhibited by voice)
12–14 hours · two weeks (weeks 242–243), plus the MAG track

blocks.text: Materials This unit, official speeches in Arabic published on institutional sites (Appendix C), session with the tutor
Targets. At the end of the lesson you know:
1. recognising the parties to an official speech and the protocol formulas;
2. recognizing and naming in Arabic the main rhetorical figures (repection, parallelism, antithesis, question
rhetoric, prose rhyme, quotation, metaphor, hyperbole, euphemism);
3. to distinguish in a speech the precise commitments from vague formulas, with the instruments of modality (B2-09);
4. translating a discourse by keeping the register and figures, without adding or removing emphasis;
5. write a short rhetorical analysis of a real public speech.
Two-week plan.

4. The method in five questions
1. Who is this, to whom, on what occasion? (genre: national party, summit, campaign, inauguration)
2. What's the central message? (in a sentence)
3. What figures does he use, and why? (two or three, with examples and function)
4. What does he really promise? (precise commitments: who, what, when, how much; vague formulas: B2-09)
5. What doesn't he say? (themes absent, missing numbers, euphemisms: B2-12)
5. Pronunciation

Read a speech like a speaker. The official speeches are read in fuṣḥā with desinence, slowly, with marked pauses. Practice Reading 1: Mark short breaks with a bar (/) and two bars (//) long breaks; slow down on the series of three; raises the voice on the second part of the antithesis; make the rhyme of sajʿ. Then read again how a journalist would read it, quoting it in a service: faster, without emphasis.
